EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong mid- and upper-level trough for early July was centered over the Plains and gradually moved eastward toward the Ohio Valley on July 1st and 2nd, 2023. A meandering surface frontal boundary gradually became more well defined throughout this period, with a warm front lifting through the Ohio Valley on July 1st before a series of remnant outflow boundaries and a convectively-enhanced cold frontal passage occurred July 2nd into the morning hours of July 3rd. Across central Kentucky and southern Indiana, there was ample fuel for convection, as temperatures in the mid-to-upper 80s and lower 90s and dewpoints in the low-to-mid 60s allowed for the development of over 2500 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Since there was initially no predominant organizing feature for convection, multiple waves of showers and thunderstorms moved across the region on July 1st, producing intermittent instances of damaging straight-line winds and near-severe hail, primarily across southern Indiana. However, as the main trough and the surface cold front moved into the region on July 2nd, convection was better organized thanks to 40-45 knots of effective bulk shear in addition to moderate to high levels of instability. Convective development on July 2nd began during the early afternoon hours across southwestern Indiana and western Kentucky. Initially, convective mode was predominantly cellular, but cells gradually grew upscale through the afternoon into clusters and larger quasi-linear structures. Downdraft CAPE was over 1000 J/kg and significant hail parameter values exceeded 1 through most of the area; accordingly, strong to damaging winds and hail were the primary severe hazards observed during the afternoon and evening hours on July 2nd. However, there was just enough low-level helicity to facilitate the development of two weak tornadoes, one in Anderson County and the other in Casey County. Storms gradually subsided after sunset, with the severe threat ending across the region by midnight on July 3rd..
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down in eastern Jefferson County near Brooksburg.

event_description: DECLARING DISASTER EMERGENCIES IN CLAY FOUNTAIN GIBSON JOHNSON MARTIN SPENCER VERMILLION AND VIGO COUNTIES DUE TO SEVERE WEATHER
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong mid- and upper-level trough for early July was centered over the Plains and gradually moved eastward toward the Ohio Valley on July 1st and 2nd, 2023. A meandering surface frontal boundary gradually became more well defined throughout this period, with a warm front lifting through the Ohio Valley on July 1st before a series of remnant outflow boundaries and a convectively-enhanced cold frontal passage occurred July 2nd into the morning hours of July 3rd. Across central Kentucky and southern Indiana, there was ample fuel for convection, as temperatures in the mid-to-upper 80s and lower 90s and dewpoints in the low-to-mid 60s allowed for the development of over 2500 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Since there was initially no predominant organizing feature for convection, multiple waves of showers and thunderstorms moved across the region on July 1st, producing intermittent instances of damaging straight-line winds and near-severe hail, primarily across southern Indiana. However, as the main trough and the surface cold front moved into the region on July 2nd, convection was better organized thanks to 40-45 knots of effective bulk shear in addition to moderate to high levels of instability. Convective development on July 2nd began during the early afternoon hours across southwestern Indiana and western Kentucky. Initially, convective mode was predominantly cellular, but cells gradually grew upscale through the afternoon into clusters and larger quasi-linear structures. Downdraft CAPE was over 1000 J/kg and significant hail parameter values exceeded 1 through most of the area; accordingly, strong to damaging winds and hail were the primary severe hazards observed during the afternoon and evening hours on July 2nd. However, there was just enough low-level helicity to facilitate the development of two weak tornadoes, one in Anderson County and the other in Casey County. Storms gradually subsided after sunset, with the severe threat ending across the region by midnight on July 3rd..
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down near Oriole.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm rapidly strengthened during the early morning hours, producing hail up to the size of golf balls and damaging winds from 70 to 80 mph. During the mid-morning hours, a cluster of severe thunderstorms evolved into a thunderstorm complex that produced mainly damaging winds. The severe weather reports were concentrated mainly east of a line from Princeton to Evansville, including the eastern Evansville metro area. The persistence of the thunderstorm clusters over the same areas resulted in pockets of flash flooding. This morning round of severe thunderstorms was associated with a southwest wind flow of hot and humid air ahead of a cold front that extended from Wisconsin to northwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was flowing across Highway 61 south of Petersburg, prompting the closure of the road. Water was over many roads in Petersburg. Personal weather stations in the Petersburg area measured 4 to 6.5 inches during the morning and early afternoon hours. Around 4 inches fell within 90 minutes.

event_description: DECLARING DISASTER EMERGENCIES IN CLAY FOUNTAIN GIBSON JOHNSON MARTIN SPENCER VERMILLION AND VIGO COUNTIES DUE TO SEVERE WEATHER
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two more rounds of severe thunderstorms occurred after the morning round. During the mid-afternoon hours, an organized squall line moved southward across southwest Indiana. Isolated wind damage was reported, with gusts up to 70 mph at a few locations. During the early evening, a couple of isolated severe thunderstorms tracked southeast across southwest Indiana. These storms packed wind gusts up to 80 mph along with hail up to the size of quarters. The combination of the three rounds of severe storms resulted in rather widespread power outages across southwest Indiana.  The storms occurred ahead of a southeastward moving cold front that extended from northern Illinois through central Missouri. A low amplitude 500 mb shortwave overspread parts of central Illinois and Indiana during the evening, accompanied by 60 to 70 knots of mid-level wind flow. The strong wind shear supported organized storm structures, including lines and elevated supercells. Even though earlier rounds of storms stabilized the atmosphere, a strengthening low-level jet favored regeneration of convection along and atop the outflow-cooled air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was flowing over Highway 64 near the Gibson County line, east of Oakland City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A bowing line of severe thunderstorms moved rapidly east-northeast out of southeast Illinois across extreme southwest Indiana. This line produced wind gusts up to 70 mph from the Wabash River east to the Evansville metro area. The storms developed in response to a rather amplified 500 mb shortwave trough that progressed east into Iowa and Missouri by nightfall. With daytime heating, the atmosphere became very unstable in the afternoon. Mixed-layer capes were around 3000 j/kg late in the day. A belt of 35 to 45 knot mid-level west-southwesterly winds resulted in sufficient deep-layer wind shear for organized storm structures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated a wind gust to 70 mph.

Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of Newton and northwest Jasper Counties, most notably the community of Lake Village. After forming and causing EF-3 damage in Kankakee County, Illinois, this tornado crossed into Newton County between W 800 N Road and W 900 N Road near N 650 W Road. Upon entering the county, the tornado destroyed multiple outbuildings and significantly damaged multiple homes. On N 600 W Road, multiple homes were completely destroyed with debris blown clear of the foundations, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds. Nearby forested areas had almost all trees snapped or uprooted with some trees remaining standing with only stubs of a few large branches remaining, likely due to extensive lifted debris. Multiple homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was destroyed along N 500 W Road and along and near N 400 W Road. As the tornado crossed US-41 into the south side of Lake Village, it widened to approximately 1100 yards while damaging the roof and canopy of a gas station and a nearby retail building. Further north along N 300 W Road, multiple blocks of homes had significant roof damage and almost all trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado continued eastward into a wooded area near the Lugene Links Golf Course, where a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted. As the tornado neared W 950 N Road and N 150 W Road, a few homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was completely destroyed. The tornado continued to produce damage to trees and outbuildings as it traveled northeastward through mainly rural portions of northern Newton County and northern portions of Roselawn. The tornado continued into Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Kankakee County and the other two near Lake Village.
